name: Brokskat
confidence_why: The only work that marks Brokskat accent, Schmidt and Kaul 2008, does so in a semi-phonemic word list whose marked syllable varies from word to word and states outright that it could not tell stress from pitch, while Ramaswami 1975, 1982 and 1989 and Sharma 1998 say nothing about stress at all, so neither the placement nor the type of the system can be stated.
catalog_citation: Schmidt, Ruth Laila & Vijay Kumar Kaul. 2008. A comparative analysis of Shina and Kashmiri vocabularies. Acta Orientalia 69: 231-301. Open access:https://journals.uio.no/actaorientalia/article/view/7372/6759
catalog_locator: p. 234 main text and p. 234 fn. 5; Brokskat column of Table 2, pp. 258-282.
catalog_quote: The pitch accent is shown in the Gilgiti, Kohistani, Guresi, Astori and Drasi entries. The phonemic inventory for Brokskat is not finalized, and the transcription of Brokskat is semi-phonemic. A falling pitch could be heard on some items, but we could not hear a rising pitch on any item, and could not exclude the possibility that the falling pitch resulted from list intonation. Therefore, stress, not pitch, is marked in the Brokskat list. [fn. 5] Every Shina word contains one accented syllable. In short syllables, the accent is realized as a high pitch and is shown as an acute accent over the vowel (ázo 'rain'). The accent need not be written on short monosyllables. Long syllables, written with double vowels, normally carry the word accent. Except in Brokskat, long vowels may have a high falling pitch, shown as an acute accent on the first vowel, or mora (táaro 'star'); or a low rising pitch, shown as an acute accent on the second vowel or mora (baál 'child'). Unaccented long vowels have been documented for Kohistani, but not for the remaining dialects.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source establishes the NATURE of Brokskat word accent, not its position: unlike all other Shina dialects (which have a moraic pitch accent with falling vs. rising contrast on long vowels), Brokskat showed no rising pitch and only a doubtful falling pitch, so the authors treat it as a stress language and mark stress (apostrophe before the stressed syllable) in their 297-item Brokskat list. No placement rule is stated anywhere in the article. In Table 2 the marked Brokskat forms fall on the initial syllable in many items ('fokur 'hair', 'kuto 'knee', 'nuto 'nose', 'baayo 'brother', 'naaro 'stone', 'bono 'big') and on a non-initial syllable in many others (sam'dal 'moustache', si'naa 'child', mu'ley 'daughter', man'nili 'bread', pi'nili 'ant', bi'loo 'cat', u'this 'to stand', zaa'zis 'to walk'); about 77 of 309 rows carry a mark, the rest (mostly monosyllables or unmarked) do not. Taken at face value the list shows lexically variable stress, but that is my reading of the data, not the authors' statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Brokskat. The authors flag their Brokskat transcription as 'semi-phonemic' and the inventory as 'not finalized'; the falling pitch heard on some items may be list intonation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms from a 280/297-item core-vocabulary list elicited in Urdu (early 1980s, transcribed by V. K. Kaul; speakers from Garkhon and Batalik). Second-hand snippets of Schmidt 2004 (Saxena ed., pp. 33-55) say the same: for the Brokskat outlier a [falling] tone 'can be heard in long vowels, but there is no trace of a rising tone', and 'Except in Brokskat, long vowels may have a high pitch.. or a low pitch'. Ramaswami's own CIIL descriptions (1975 Phonetic Reader, 1982 Grammar, 1989 Dictionary) are silent on stress and mark none.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand sources describe the Brokskat of Garkhon/Batalik (Dah-Hanu area, Kargil district, Ladakh), i.e. brok1247 itself: Ramaswami's data are from Garkhon (informant Gulam Rahim, Phonetic Reader p. 2); Schmidt & Kaul's Brokskat list was provided by Stanzin Khurpa of Garkhon and Miskin Tshiring of Batalik (2008: 232 n. 2). No separate glottocode involved. Note that the Rosetta Project mis-tags Sharma 1998 (Brok-skad = Brokskat) under ISO 'bro' (Brokkat of Bhutan).
